questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Recovery-Oriented Mental Health Nursing
questions.stem: A person with recurrent depression says, 'I am more than this illness.' Which nursing response best reflects recovery-oriented practice?

options.text: Ask about the person's strengths, goals and what has helped previously.
Focus the discussion on symptoms that must be eliminated.
Explain that recovery depends mainly on medication adherence.
Redirect the conversation to the diagnosis.

questions.rationale: Recovery-oriented care sees the person beyond diagnosis and supports hope, identity, choice and meaningful goals.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Recovery-Oriented Mental Health Nursing
questions.stem: Which statement best describes recovery in mental health care?

options.text: Recovery always means complete absence of symptoms.
Recovery may involve living a meaningful and self-directed life while managing ongoing symptoms.
Recovery is determined only by the clinician.
Recovery begins after treatment has ended.

questions.rationale: Recovery is personal and may occur even when some symptoms remain.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Recovery-Oriented Mental Health Nursing
questions.stem: A nurse hears a colleague describe a person as 'a manipulative schizophrenic.' What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: Ignore the comment because it is informal.
Repeat the description in the clinical notes.
Challenge the stigmatising language and encourage person-first, objective communication.
Avoid discussing the person with the colleague.

questions.rationale: Stigmatising labels can damage care and should be replaced with respectful, person-centred language.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Recovery-Oriented Mental Health Nursing
questions.stem: A patient reports low mood, chronic pain, poor sleep and recent housing insecurity. Which assessment approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Focus only on the depressive symptoms.
Refer all social concerns to another service without discussion.
Delay physical assessment until mood improves.
Explore physical health, sleep, pain, medication, substance use and social conditions together.

questions.rationale: Mental and physical health are interconnected, and social conditions may strongly influence wellbeing.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Recovery-Oriented Mental Health Nursing
questions.stem: Which action best supports a person's autonomy?

options.text: Providing information and involving the person in choices within safety and legal limits.
Making decisions quickly on the person's behalf.
Asking family members to decide routinely.

questions.rationale: Recovery-oriented care treats the person as an active partner.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Recovery-Oriented Mental Health Nursing
questions.stem: A person says that returning to study is an important goal. How should the nurse respond?

options.text: Explain that education should wait until all symptoms resolve.
Include the goal in care planning and explore practical supports.
Tell the person to discuss it after discharge.

questions.rationale: Meaningful personal goals are central to recovery-oriented practice.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Recovery-Oriented Mental Health Nursing
questions.stem: Which factor may influence mental health?

options.text: Biological, psychological, social, cultural and environmental factors.

questions.rationale: Mental health exists on a continuum and is influenced by multiple interacting factors.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Recovery-Oriented Mental Health Nursing
questions.stem: A person with a long-term mental health condition is working, maintaining relationships and managing symptoms. What does this illustrate?

options.text: A person may live well while managing an ongoing condition.

questions.rationale: Wellbeing and recovery are possible alongside long-term symptoms or treatment.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Recovery-Oriented Mental Health Nursing
questions.stem: A nurse notices that a patient with anxiety is also experiencing severe insomnia and poor nutrition. What should the care plan include?

options.text: Sleep, nutrition and physical-health needs as well as emotional distress.

questions.rationale: Holistic mental health care addresses physical, psychological and social needs.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Recovery-Oriented Mental Health Nursing
questions.stem: Which nursing statement is most strengths-based?

options.text: 'What problems have you caused at home?'
'What has helped you cope during difficult times before?'
'You need to accept that you are unwell.'

questions.rationale: Strengths-based care explores capabilities, supports and previous successful coping.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Recovery-Oriented Mental Health Nursing
questions.stem: A person from a cultural background unfamiliar to the nurse describes distress in physical terms. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume the person is avoiding mental-health discussion.
Explore the person's explanation of the symptoms and complete both physical and mental-health assessment.

questions.rationale: Culture can shape how distress is understood and expressed; assessment should remain respectful and holistic.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Recovery-Oriented Mental Health Nursing
questions.stem: A patient says stigma has prevented them from seeking help. Which response is most therapeutic?

options.text: 'You should not worry about other people's opinions.'
'It sounds as though fear of judgement has made it harder to seek support.'

questions.rationale: Validation acknowledges the person's experience without minimising it.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Recovery-Oriented Mental Health Nursing
questions.stem: Which action is inconsistent with recovery-oriented practice?

options.text: Defining the person mainly by diagnosis.

questions.rationale: Recovery-oriented practice recognises the whole person, not only the diagnosis.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Recovery-Oriented Mental Health Nursing
questions.stem: A person wishes to involve a trusted family member in care planning. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Support involvement with the person's consent and clarify the family member's role.
Ask the family to make final decisions.

questions.rationale: Family participation should be guided by the person's preferences, consent and safety needs.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Recovery-Oriented Mental Health Nursing
questions.stem: A nurse is planning care with a person who has repeated admissions. What is the most useful first question?

options.text: 'What was happening before the recent difficulties, and what support would be useful now?'
'Which diagnosis do you think is most accurate?'

questions.rationale: A collaborative, non-judgemental question explores context and needed support.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Recovery-Oriented Mental Health Nursing
questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects person-centred mental health care?

options.text: The person follows every recommendation without question.
The nurse completes the assessment quickly.
The care plan reflects the person's strengths, needs, preferences and safety concerns.

questions.rationale: Person-centred care is individualised and collaborative.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Recovery-Oriented Mental Health Nursing
questions.stem: A person says spirituality is important to recovery. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Explore how spirituality supports the person and include it in care where appropriate.
Avoid the topic because it is not clinical.
Assume the person belongs to a particular faith.

questions.rationale: Meaning, identity and cultural or spiritual supports may be important recovery resources.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Recovery-Oriented Mental Health Nursing
questions.stem: A nurse focuses only on psychiatric symptoms and overlooks uncontrolled diabetes. What is the main concern?

options.text: The mental-health assessment will be shorter.
Physical-health needs may be missed, worsening overall outcomes.
The person may become more independent.

questions.rationale: Mental and physical healthcare should be integrated.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Recovery-Oriented Mental Health Nursing
questions.stem: Which statement best challenges discrimination?

options.text: 'Risk should be assessed individually rather than assumed from a diagnosis.'
'Families should make decisions for most patients.'

questions.rationale: Individual assessment avoids harmful stereotypes.

questions.sectionLabel: Foundations of Recovery-Oriented Mental Health Nursing
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates recovery-oriented nursing?

options.text: The nurse controls all treatment decisions.
The person develops hope, participates in care and pursues personally meaningful goals safely.

questions.rationale: Recovery-oriented care supports participation, hope and meaningful life goals.

questions.sectionLabel: Therapeutic Communication and Professional Relationships
questions.stem: A woman says, 'Nothing will ever get better.' Which response is most therapeutic?

options.text: 'It sounds as though things feel hopeless. Can you tell me more about what has been happening?'
'You will be fine once treatment starts.'

questions.rationale: The response validates distress and invites further assessment without false reassurance.

questions.sectionLabel: Therapeutic Communication and Professional Relationships
questions.stem: Which communication technique demonstrates active listening?

options.text: Changing the subject when emotion increases.
Reflecting the person's meaning and asking for clarification.

questions.rationale: Reflection and clarification communicate attention and help organise thoughts.

questions.sectionLabel: Therapeutic Communication and Professional Relationships
questions.stem: A suspicious patient answers questions briefly and appears overwhelmed. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Use calm, simple language and allow trust to develop gradually.

questions.rationale: A calm, paced approach reduces pressure and supports trust.

questions.sectionLabel: Therapeutic Communication and Professional Relationships
questions.stem: Which response is non-therapeutic?

options.text: 'Tell me more about what worries you.'
'I can see that this is difficult.'
'There is no reason to feel anxious.'

questions.rationale: Dismissing emotion can close communication.

questions.sectionLabel: Therapeutic Communication and Professional Relationships
questions.stem: A patient becomes silent and tearful. What is the most appropriate nursing action?

options.text: Remain present and allow time before gently inviting the person to continue.

questions.rationale: Therapeutic silence can communicate support and allow emotional processing.

questions.sectionLabel: Therapeutic Communication and Professional Relationships
questions.stem: A person says, 'No one listens to me.' Which response best demonstrates empathy?
questions.rationale: Empathy acknowledges the person's emotional experience.

questions.sectionLabel: Therapeutic Communication and Professional Relationships
questions.stem: A patient offers the nurse an expensive personal gift. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Accept it but do not tell colleagues.
Decline respectfully and explain professional boundaries.
Exchange a gift of similar value.

questions.rationale: Professional boundaries protect both the person and nurse.

questions.sectionLabel: Therapeutic Communication and Professional Relationships
questions.stem: Which behaviour is a boundary concern?

options.text: Sharing personal financial problems and asking the patient for help.

questions.rationale: Personal financial involvement is outside the therapeutic role.

questions.sectionLabel: Therapeutic Communication and Professional Relationships
questions.stem: A patient asks to connect with the nurse on social media after discharge. What is the best response?

options.text: Maintain professional boundaries and decline the request.
Accept after the therapeutic relationship ends.
Ask the patient to contact another nurse.

questions.rationale: Relationships outside the therapeutic role can blur boundaries and create harm.

questions.sectionLabel: Therapeutic Communication and Professional Relationships
questions.stem: A person experiencing panic is struggling to process information. How should the nurse communicate?

options.text: Provide a detailed explanation of anxiety theory.
Use short, calm statements and one question at a time.
Ask the family to answer all questions.

questions.rationale: Simple, calm communication is easier to process during severe anxiety.

questions.sectionLabel: Therapeutic Communication and Professional Relationships
questions.stem: A patient says, 'The staff are poisoning my food.' What is the most appropriate response?

options.text: 'That is impossible and you are mistaken.'
'I understand that the food feels unsafe to you. Can you tell me what makes you think that?'

questions.rationale: The nurse acknowledges the fear without agreeing with or arguing about the belief.

questions.sectionLabel: Therapeutic Communication and Professional Relationships
questions.stem: Which statement is an example of summarising?

options.text: 'You have described poor sleep, increasing worry and difficulty attending work.'

questions.rationale: Summarising brings together key information and checks shared understanding.

questions.sectionLabel: Therapeutic Communication and Professional Relationships
questions.stem: A nurse feels unusually protective of one patient and begins spending extra time with them. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Reflect on the response, seek supervision and restore consistent boundaries.
Tell the patient about the feelings.

questions.rationale: Self-awareness and supervision help prevent boundary drift.

questions.sectionLabel: Therapeutic Communication and Professional Relationships
questions.stem: Which question is most therapeutic when exploring distress?

options.text: 'What was happening when the distress became worse?'
'You will take the medicine, won't you?'

questions.rationale: An open, non-judgemental question supports exploration.

questions.sectionLabel: Therapeutic Communication and Professional Relationships
questions.stem: A patient asks the nurse to keep a plan to self-harm secret. What is the appropriate response?

options.text: Explain that immediate safety concerns cannot remain confidential and take protective action.
Wait until the patient repeats the statement.

questions.rationale: Confidentiality has limits when there is serious risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Therapeutic Communication and Professional Relationships
questions.stem: Which behaviour best supports trust?

options.text: Making promises the nurse cannot guarantee.
Sharing private information to build closeness.
Being consistent, honest and clear about the nurse's role.

questions.rationale: Trust develops through consistency, honesty and reliability.

questions.sectionLabel: Therapeutic Communication and Professional Relationships
questions.stem: A person becomes withdrawn when asked several questions. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Reduce the number of questions, acknowledge the discomfort and allow time.
Increase the pace to complete the assessment.
Ask the family to answer instead.

questions.rationale: Communication should be adapted to the person's state.

questions.sectionLabel: Therapeutic Communication and Professional Relationships
questions.stem: Which response uses clarification?

options.text: 'When you say you feel unsafe, what does unsafe mean for you?'

questions.rationale: Clarification checks the meaning of the person's words.

questions.sectionLabel: Therapeutic Communication and Professional Relationships
questions.stem: A patient repeatedly asks for personal information about the nurse. What is the best response?

options.text: Provide detailed information to build trust.
Acknowledge the question and redirect to the patient's needs while maintaining boundaries.
Ask the patient why they are being intrusive.

questions.rationale: Limited, purposeful responses may be appropriate, but the focus remains on the person receiving care.

questions.sectionLabel: Therapeutic Communication and Professional Relationships
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates effective therapeutic communication?

options.text: The patient agrees with the nurse.
The person feels heard, shares relevant information and participates in planning.

questions.rationale: Therapeutic communication supports understanding, assessment and collaboration.

questions.sectionLabel: Mental Health Assessment and Common Conditions
questions.stem: Which component is included in a mental state examination?

options.text: Appearance, behaviour, speech, mood, thought, perception, cognition, insight and judgement.

questions.rationale: The mental state examination systematically describes current mental functioning.

questions.sectionLabel: Mental Health Assessment and Common Conditions
questions.stem: A patient speaks very rapidly, sleeps two hours each night and has begun spending large amounts of money. What condition should the nurse consider?
questions.rationale: Elevated mood, reduced sleep, rapid speech and risky behaviour are characteristic of mania.

questions.sectionLabel: Mental Health Assessment and Common Conditions
questions.stem: A person reports hearing a voice telling them to harm themselves. What should the nurse ask first?

options.text: Why the person is imagining the voice.
What the voice says, whether the person intends to act and whether they have access to means.

questions.rationale: Command hallucinations require direct assessment of content, intent, means and ability to resist.

questions.sectionLabel: Mental Health Assessment and Common Conditions
questions.stem: A patient says the television is sending personal messages. How should the nurse respond?

options.text: Agree that the messages are real.
Tell the patient the belief is irrational.
Turn off the television and end the discussion.
Explore the experience and assess distress and safety without arguing about the belief.

questions.rationale: The nurse assesses meaning and risk without reinforcing or confronting the delusion.

questions.sectionLabel: Mental Health Assessment and Common Conditions
questions.stem: Which finding is most consistent with depression?

options.text: Persistent low mood, loss of interest, sleep change and hopelessness.
Elevated mood and reduced need for sleep.

questions.rationale: These are common depressive symptoms.

questions.sectionLabel: Mental Health Assessment and Common Conditions
questions.stem: A patient develops sudden confusion and fluctuating attention after surgery. What should the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Acute fluctuating confusion suggests delirium, often caused by physical illness or medication.

questions.sectionLabel: Mental Health Assessment and Common Conditions
questions.stem: Which feature is more typical of dementia than delirium?
questions.rationale: Dementia usually develops gradually, while delirium is acute and fluctuating.

questions.sectionLabel: Mental Health Assessment and Common Conditions
questions.stem: A patient is restless, sweating and tremulous after abruptly stopping alcohol. What should the nurse consider?

options.text: Alcohol withdrawal requiring assessment and monitoring.

questions.rationale: Withdrawal can become severe and requires timely clinical assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Mental Health Assessment and Common Conditions
questions.stem: Which finding may indicate a panic attack?

options.text: Sudden intense fear, palpitations, breathlessness and a sense of losing control.

questions.rationale: Panic attacks involve abrupt severe anxiety with physical symptoms.

questions.sectionLabel: Mental Health Assessment and Common Conditions
questions.stem: A nurse documents, 'Patient is difficult and manipulative.' What is the main problem?

options.text: The language is subjective and should be replaced with objective observations.
The note should include the nurse's feelings.

questions.rationale: Documentation should describe behaviour and statements objectively.

questions.sectionLabel: Mental Health Assessment and Common Conditions
questions.stem: A patient says, 'I have no energy and nothing matters.' Which additional question is most important?

options.text: 'Have you had thoughts of harming yourself or not wanting to live?'

questions.rationale: Hopelessness can be associated with suicide risk and requires direct assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Mental Health Assessment and Common Conditions
questions.stem: Which observation describes affect?
questions.rationale: Affect is the outwardly observed emotional expression.

questions.sectionLabel: Mental Health Assessment and Common Conditions
questions.stem: A patient appears to respond to unseen stimuli but denies hallucinations. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Describe the observed behaviour and continue respectful assessment.
Ask other patients what they observed.

questions.rationale: Observation and conversation should be used together, and findings documented objectively.

questions.sectionLabel: Mental Health Assessment and Common Conditions
questions.stem: A person reports daily cannabis use and increasing paranoia. What is the best nursing approach?

options.text: Assume the substance use is unrelated.
Assess timing, amount, mental-state changes and safety, and seek further review.
Tell the person to stop immediately and end the assessment.

questions.rationale: Substance use can affect perception and behaviour and should be assessed carefully.

questions.sectionLabel: Mental Health Assessment and Common Conditions
questions.stem: Which finding most strongly suggests disorganised thought form?

options.text: The person believes neighbours are watching them.
Speech is difficult to follow because ideas are loosely connected.
The person hears music when alone.

questions.rationale: Thought form refers to the organisation and flow of ideas.

questions.sectionLabel: Mental Health Assessment and Common Conditions
questions.stem: A patient with depression has stopped eating and drinking. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ask the family to bring favourite foods.
Assess hydration, nutrition, physical health and immediate risk.

questions.rationale: Mental-health assessment must include physical-health consequences and safety.

questions.sectionLabel: Mental Health Assessment and Common Conditions
questions.stem: A patient has reduced concentration, poor sleep and anxiety following bereavement. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.text: Explore duration, severity, functioning, supports and risk without making premature conclusions.
Assume a psychiatric disorder is present.
Tell the person grief should be over.

questions.rationale: Assessment should consider context, function and risk rather than label normal or complicated responses prematurely.

questions.sectionLabel: Mental Health Assessment and Common Conditions
questions.stem: Which finding requires urgent medical review rather than routine psychiatric follow-up?

options.text: New confusion with fever and reduced oxygen saturation.

questions.rationale: Acute cognitive change with physical abnormalities may indicate delirium or medical deterioration.

questions.sectionLabel: Mental Health Assessment and Common Conditions
questions.stem: A patient describes feeling watched but is unsure whether the belief is accurate. What does this suggest about insight?

options.text: Judgement is normal in all areas.

questions.rationale: Questioning one's own interpretation can indicate partial insight.

questions.sectionLabel: Mental Health Assessment and Common Conditions
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates a complete basic mental-health assessment?

options.text: The person's story, mental state, physical health, substance use, function and current risks are assessed collaboratively.

questions.rationale: A comprehensive assessment integrates observation, conversation, physical health and risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Crisis, Safety and Psychotropic Medication
questions.stem: A patient says, 'I have been thinking about ending my life.' What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ask directly about plan, intent, means, timing, past behaviour and protective factors.
Avoid further questions to prevent increasing the risk.
Reassure the patient that things will improve.
Ask the family to complete the assessment.

questions.rationale: Direct suicide assessment does not create suicidal ideas and is essential for determining risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Crisis, Safety and Psychotropic Medication
questions.stem: Which finding indicates the highest immediate suicide risk?

options.text: Passive thoughts with no plan and strong supports.
A specific plan, intent to act and access to the means.

questions.rationale: Plan, intent and access to means indicate high immediate risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Crisis, Safety and Psychotropic Medication
questions.stem: A patient becomes agitated, pacing and shouting. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Reduce stimulation, maintain a safe distance, use a calm tone and offer clear choices.
Ask several staff to surround the patient.

questions.rationale: Early de-escalation uses calm communication, respectful distance and reduced stimulation.

questions.sectionLabel: Crisis, Safety and Psychotropic Medication
questions.stem: Which action reflects least restrictive practice?

options.text: Using restraint as soon as a person refuses care.
Trying verbal de-escalation, environmental change and support before restrictive measures when safe.

questions.rationale: Restriction should be used only when less restrictive measures are insufficient for serious immediate risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Crisis, Safety and Psychotropic Medication
questions.stem: A patient states an intention to attack another person and moves toward them. What is the priority?

options.text: Activate the emergency safety plan, protect others and seek immediate support.
Ask the patient to write down the feelings.
Leave the area without warning others.

questions.rationale: An immediate threat of violence requires urgent safety action.

questions.sectionLabel: Crisis, Safety and Psychotropic Medication
questions.stem: Which environment best supports de-escalation?

options.text: A quieter space with clear exits, reduced stimulation and appropriate staff support.

questions.rationale: Reduced stimulation and safe positioning can lower escalation risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Crisis, Safety and Psychotropic Medication
questions.stem: A patient taking an antipsychotic develops high fever, severe rigidity and altered consciousness. What should the nurse suspect?

options.text: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome requiring urgent medical care.

questions.rationale: Fever, rigidity and altered consciousness are key warning signs of neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

questions.sectionLabel: Crisis, Safety and Psychotropic Medication
questions.stem: A patient taking an antidepressant develops agitation, sweating, diarrhoea, tremor and hyperreflexia after a medication change. What should the nurse consider?
questions.rationale: This cluster is concerning for serotonin syndrome.

questions.sectionLabel: Crisis, Safety and Psychotropic Medication
questions.stem: A person taking lithium develops vomiting, coarse tremor, confusion and unsteady gait. What is the appropriate action?

options.text: Withhold the medicine according to policy and obtain urgent review for possible toxicity.
Administer the next dose with food.
Reassure the person that the effects are expected.

questions.rationale: Gastrointestinal symptoms, coarse tremor, confusion and ataxia may indicate lithium toxicity.

questions.sectionLabel: Crisis, Safety and Psychotropic Medication
questions.stem: A patient becomes excessively sedated after an anxiolytic. What should the nurse assess first?

options.text: Airway, respiratory rate, oxygenation and level of consciousness.

questions.rationale: Sedation can compromise breathing and requires immediate physiological assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Crisis, Safety and Psychotropic Medication
questions.stem: Which question should be included in violence-risk assessment?

options.text: 'Have you had thoughts of harming anyone, and do you have a plan or access to weapons?'

questions.rationale: Direct, specific questions assess thoughts, plan and means.

questions.sectionLabel: Crisis, Safety and Psychotropic Medication
questions.stem: A patient has self-inflicted injuries but denies current suicidal intent. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Discharge the patient because intent is denied.
Assess current intent, purpose of self-harm, past behaviour, supports and immediate safety needs.

questions.rationale: Self-harm and suicide risk overlap but are not identical; both require careful assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Crisis, Safety and Psychotropic Medication
questions.stem: Which action is most appropriate when a high-risk patient asks to be left alone?

options.text: Maintain the level of observation required by the safety plan and explain the reason respectfully.
Ask another patient to observe them.

questions.rationale: Safety planning may require observation while preserving dignity as much as possible.

questions.sectionLabel: Crisis, Safety and Psychotropic Medication
questions.stem: A patient in severe panic says, 'I am going to die.' What should the nurse do?

options.text: Explain that the symptoms are not serious.
Stay with the person, use calm short statements and assess physical as well as psychological causes.
Ask the patient to complete a questionnaire.

questions.rationale: The nurse should provide calm support and ensure that physical emergencies are not overlooked.

questions.sectionLabel: Crisis, Safety and Psychotropic Medication
questions.stem: Which statement about restraint is correct?

options.text: It may be used when staff are busy.
It should follow law and policy and be used only when less restrictive measures cannot manage serious immediate risk.
It is part of routine de-escalation.

questions.rationale: Restrictive interventions require strict justification, monitoring and legal compliance.

questions.sectionLabel: Crisis, Safety and Psychotropic Medication
questions.stem: A patient abruptly stops a long-term sedative medicine and develops severe agitation and tremor. What should the nurse consider?
questions.rationale: Abrupt cessation of some medicines can cause dangerous withdrawal.

questions.sectionLabel: Crisis, Safety and Psychotropic Medication
questions.stem: Which protective factor may reduce suicide risk?

options.text: A trusted support person and willingness to seek help.

questions.rationale: Support, connection and help-seeking can be protective, although they do not remove the need for assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Crisis, Safety and Psychotropic Medication
questions.stem: A suicidal patient agrees verbally to stay safe. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Rely on the verbal promise alone.
Develop an individual safety plan, reduce access to means and arrange appropriate observation and escalation.
Ask the family to take full responsibility.

questions.rationale: A verbal promise is not a substitute for comprehensive safety planning.

questions.sectionLabel: Crisis, Safety and Psychotropic Medication
questions.stem: Which documentation is most appropriate after de-escalation?

options.text: The nurse's opinion of the patient's personality.
Objective behaviour, identified triggers, interventions used, response, remaining risk and who was informed.

questions.rationale: Documentation should be factual and include risk, intervention and response.

questions.sectionLabel: Crisis, Safety and Psychotropic Medication
questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects safe crisis care?

options.text: Family members agree with the plan.
Immediate risk is assessed, dignity is preserved, the least restrictive effective response is used and treatment effects are monitored.

questions.rationale: Safe crisis care balances protection, dignity, proportionality and reassessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment, Formulation and Care Planning
questions.stem: A woman with bipolar disorder presents with two hours of sleep each night, rapid speech, impulsive spending and escalating conflict at home. Which assessment approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Integrate mental state, physical health, substance use, medication, trauma, supports, current risk and previous relapse signs.
Complete a mental state examination only.
Focus on financial behaviour because it is the main problem.
Delay risk assessment until the woman becomes calmer.

questions.rationale: A comprehensive assessment integrates current presentation with physical health, substance use, history, strengths, supports and risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment, Formulation and Care Planning
questions.stem: Which statement best describes a nursing formulation?

options.text: A diagnostic label written by the nurse.
A concise explanation linking presenting problems, contributing factors, strengths, risks and priority nursing needs.
A list of symptoms copied from the medical record.

questions.rationale: A formulation organises assessment findings into a meaningful explanation that guides care.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment, Formulation and Care Planning
questions.stem: A patient reports suicidal thoughts but denies a plan. Which factor should the nurse assess next?

options.text: Only the severity of low mood.
Whether the patient agrees with the diagnosis.
Intent, access to means, past attempts, recent triggers and protective factors.
Whether family members are available to visit.

questions.rationale: Risk formulation requires more than the presence or absence of a plan.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment, Formulation and Care Planning
questions.stem: Why should a numerical suicide-risk score not determine care by itself?

options.text: Scores are never used in mental health.
They are only useful for medication decisions.
They are legally prohibited in every jurisdiction.
They cannot fully capture changing triggers, history, protective factors and clinical judgement.

questions.rationale: Risk is dynamic and requires clinical formulation rather than reliance on one number.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment, Formulation and Care Planning
questions.stem: A patient with severe depression has stopped eating and has poorly controlled diabetes. What should the nurse prioritise?

options.text: Both immediate physical-health needs and mental-health risk.
Referral to dietetics without further assessment.

questions.rationale: International mental health practice requires integrated physical and mental healthcare.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment, Formulation and Care Planning
questions.stem: Which handover statement is most useful?

options.text: “The patient is increasingly suspicious, has slept two hours, believes neighbours are watching him, and becomes calmer when approached by one staff member.”

questions.rationale: Effective handover communicates current mental state, triggers, helpful strategies and required action objectively.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment, Formulation and Care Planning
questions.stem: A person identifies regular contact with a sibling and commitment to caring for a pet as reasons to stay safe. How should the nurse use this information?

options.text: Exclude it because protective factors do not affect risk.
Treat it as proof that suicide risk is absent.
Include it in the risk formulation and safety plan.

questions.rationale: Protective factors are important but do not eliminate the need for ongoing assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment, Formulation and Care Planning
questions.stem: A patient with mania refuses to discuss sleep because “sleep is a waste of time.” Which response is most therapeutic?

options.text: Argue that the belief is irrational.
Tell the patient that medication will solve the problem.
Explore how reduced sleep is affecting energy, judgement and safety.

questions.rationale: The nurse should explore impact and risk without confrontation.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment, Formulation and Care Planning
questions.stem: Which care plan is most actionable?

options.text: “Patient will contact the crisis line or named support if suicidal urges increase; nurse will review daily and the team will confirm medicine access before discharge.”

questions.rationale: Actionable plans specify goals, responsibilities, timeframes and practical steps.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment, Formulation and Care Planning
questions.stem: A patient’s cultural explanation of distress differs from the clinical team’s interpretation. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Explore the patient’s meaning, cultural context and help-seeking preferences while completing a safe assessment.
Ask the family to interpret the patient’s beliefs.

questions.rationale: Culturally safe assessment asks rather than assumes and incorporates the person’s perspective.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment, Formulation and Care Planning
questions.stem: A patient with psychosis reports chest pain. What is the safest nursing response?

options.text: Complete an appropriate physical assessment and escalate as indicated.
Document the complaint for the next shift.

questions.rationale: Physical symptoms should not be attributed automatically to mental illness.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment, Formulation and Care Planning
questions.stem: Which finding is a dynamic risk factor?

options.text: A past suicide attempt ten years ago.
Recent relationship breakdown with increasing alcohol use.

questions.rationale: Dynamic factors can change and may increase or reduce current risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment, Formulation and Care Planning
questions.stem: A formulation identifies insomnia, stimulant use, family conflict and missed medication as contributors to relapse. What should the plan do?

options.text: Target the identified contributors with clear interventions and responsibilities.

questions.rationale: Care planning should flow directly from the formulation.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment, Formulation and Care Planning
questions.stem: Which assessment finding should be communicated urgently?

options.text: Command hallucinations telling the patient to harm another person, with stated intent.
A request for a different room.
Past substance use without current symptoms.

questions.rationale: Command hallucinations with intent represent an immediate safety concern.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment, Formulation and Care Planning
questions.stem: A patient becomes confused after a medication change. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assume the mental illness is worsening.
Wait for the next psychiatric review.
Assess physical causes, medicines, substance use and possible delirium.

questions.rationale: Acute cognitive change requires broad assessment, including physical and medication causes.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment, Formulation and Care Planning
questions.stem: What is the main purpose of relapse-prevention planning?

options.text: To predict the exact date of relapse.
To ensure the family controls treatment.
To identify early warning signs, triggers, helpful actions and support contacts.

questions.rationale: A practical relapse plan supports early action and shared responsibility.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment, Formulation and Care Planning
questions.stem: A patient’s risk appears lower after admission. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Review what has changed, what risks remain and whether the improvement is sustainable.
Stop assessment because the risk has resolved.

questions.rationale: Risk is dynamic and must be reformulated as circumstances change.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment, Formulation and Care Planning
questions.stem: Which statement best reflects person-centred formulation?

options.text: It is written without the patient to preserve objectivity.
It combines professional assessment with the person’s own understanding, goals and strengths.

questions.rationale: Shared formulation respects the person as an active partner.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment, Formulation and Care Planning
questions.stem: A patient has no fixed address and limited transport. Why should this be included in care planning?

options.text: It is unrelated to mental health.
It is relevant only to social workers.
It may affect follow-up, medicine access, safety and relapse risk.
It should be discussed after discharge.

questions.rationale: Social circumstances influence access, continuity and risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Comprehensive Assessment, Formulation and Care Planning
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates effective comprehensive assessment?

options.text: The mental state examination is completed.
The patient agrees with every recommendation.
Mental, physical, social, cultural and risk information is integrated into a clear shared plan.

questions.rationale: The goal is a coherent, person-centred plan rather than checklist completion.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Suicide, Self-Harm and Acute Behavioural Disturbance
questions.stem: A patient states that tablets are hidden at home and will be taken after discharge. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Maintain immediate safety, do not leave the patient alone, and initiate urgent review.
Ask the patient to promise not to act.
Document the statement and continue routine care.

questions.rationale: A stated plan with access to means indicates high immediate risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Suicide, Self-Harm and Acute Behavioural Disturbance
questions.stem: Which question is essential in suicide assessment?

options.text: “Have you decided when or how you would act, and do you have access to the means?”
“Can you guarantee you will stay safe?”

questions.rationale: Direct, non-judgemental questions assess plan, timing, intent and means.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Suicide, Self-Harm and Acute Behavioural Disturbance
questions.stem: A person has self-harmed but denies wanting to die. What is the best response?

options.text: Treat the injury, assess current suicide risk and explore the function of self-harm without punishment.
Discharge once the wound is treated.

questions.rationale: Self-harm may serve different functions and still requires full risk assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Suicide, Self-Harm and Acute Behavioural Disturbance
questions.stem: Which observation plan is most appropriate?

options.text: The highest level for every patient.
Observation only when the patient is awake.
A purposeful level linked to current risk, reviewed and adjusted as the situation changes.

questions.rationale: Observation should be proportionate, purposeful and regularly reviewed.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Suicide, Self-Harm and Acute Behavioural Disturbance
questions.stem: A patient is pacing, shouting and clenching fists. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Reduce stimulation, maintain safe distance, offer clear choices and call for support early.
Move closer and challenge the behaviour.
Ask the patient to explain everything immediately.

questions.rationale: Early de-escalation can reduce risk while preserving dignity.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Suicide, Self-Harm and Acute Behavioural Disturbance
questions.stem: A patient threatens another person and has access to a weapon. What is the priority?

options.text: Activate the emergency safety plan and protect those at risk.
Wait for the patient to calm independently.

questions.rationale: An immediate credible threat requires urgent protective action.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Suicide, Self-Harm and Acute Behavioural Disturbance
questions.stem: Which factor increases short-term suicide risk?

options.text: Recent loss, intoxication and access to lethal means.

questions.rationale: Recent loss, intoxication and means can significantly increase immediate risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Suicide, Self-Harm and Acute Behavioural Disturbance
questions.stem: A patient asks to leave despite being under involuntary care. What should an IQN do?

options.text: Use the law from the nurse’s previous country.
Check the local legal status, policy and senior advice before acting.

questions.rationale: Legal requirements differ by jurisdiction and must be confirmed locally.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Suicide, Self-Harm and Acute Behavioural Disturbance
questions.stem: Which action best supports collaborative safety planning?

options.text: Identifying warning signs, coping strategies, support contacts and ways to reduce access to means together.
Creating a plan without the patient.
Giving the patient a generic leaflet.

questions.rationale: Safety planning should be practical, personalised and collaborative.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Suicide, Self-Harm and Acute Behavioural Disturbance
questions.stem: When is restrictive intervention justified?

options.text: When serious immediate risk cannot be managed by less restrictive measures and legal requirements are met.
When the patient is verbally rude.

questions.rationale: Restriction must be necessary, proportionate, lawful and monitored.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Suicide, Self-Harm and Acute Behavioural Disturbance
questions.stem: A patient becomes more agitated when several staff surround them. What should the team do?

options.text: Add more staff to show authority.
Reduce crowding, clarify one lead communicator and maintain safe exit access.

questions.rationale: Crowding and mixed messages can escalate distress.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Suicide, Self-Harm and Acute Behavioural Disturbance
questions.stem: Which documentation is required after restraint?

options.text: Only the start and end time.
A brief note that the patient was aggressive.
Legal basis, alternatives attempted, monitoring, injuries, response and post-event review.

questions.rationale: Restrictive interventions require detailed, objective and legally compliant documentation.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Suicide, Self-Harm and Acute Behavioural Disturbance
questions.stem: A patient with command hallucinations says, “The voice tells me to jump, but I do not want to.” What should the nurse assess?

options.text: Content, frequency, ability to resist, intent, access and protective factors.
Whether family members also hear voices.

questions.rationale: Command hallucinations require direct assessment of safety implications.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Suicide, Self-Harm and Acute Behavioural Disturbance
questions.stem: A patient under close observation appears calmer. What should happen next?

options.text: Review current risk, recent behaviour and protective factors before changing the plan.
Ask the patient to choose the observation level.

questions.rationale: Observation levels should change only after structured review.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Suicide, Self-Harm and Acute Behavioural Disturbance
questions.stem: Which response is least therapeutic after self-harm?

options.text: Using a punitive tone and removing privileges automatically.

questions.rationale: Punitive responses increase shame and undermine therapeutic engagement.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Suicide, Self-Harm and Acute Behavioural Disturbance
questions.stem: A patient becomes intoxicated and increasingly aggressive. What should the nurse consider?

options.text: Discharge as soon as the patient quietens.
Both immediate violence risk and possible medical complications of intoxication.

questions.rationale: Substance effects can increase risk and require physical as well as behavioural assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Suicide, Self-Harm and Acute Behavioural Disturbance
questions.stem: What is the purpose of post-event debriefing?

options.text: To review what happened, support those involved and identify learning for future safety.

questions.rationale: Debriefing supports recovery, staff wellbeing and system learning.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Suicide, Self-Harm and Acute Behavioural Disturbance
questions.stem: A patient refuses family involvement in safety planning. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Respect confidentiality unless lawful disclosure is required to prevent serious harm, and explore other supports.
Ask the family to attend secretly.

questions.rationale: Consent and confidentiality should be respected while legal safety duties are considered.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Suicide, Self-Harm and Acute Behavioural Disturbance
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates effective crisis management?

options.text: Immediate risk is reduced through proportionate action while dignity, engagement and review are maintained.
The family agrees with the plan.

questions.rationale: Crisis care balances safety, least restriction and therapeutic engagement.

questions.sectionLabel: Managing Suicide, Self-Harm and Acute Behavioural Disturbance
questions.stem: A patient’s suicide risk rises after receiving unexpected legal news. What does this illustrate?

options.text: Dynamic triggers can rapidly alter risk and require reformulation.

questions.rationale: Risk changes with circumstances and must be reassessed.

questions.sectionLabel: Psychopharmacology, Physical Health and Co-occurring Conditions
questions.stem: A patient taking lithium develops vomiting, coarse tremor and confusion after several days of dehydration. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Withhold further doses according to policy and arrange urgent medical review and blood testing.
Give the next dose with food.
Reassure the patient that these effects are expected.

questions.rationale: The symptoms are consistent with lithium toxicity.

questions.sectionLabel: Psychopharmacology, Physical Health and Co-occurring Conditions
questions.stem: Which monitoring is required for ongoing lithium therapy?

options.text: Blood levels, renal function, thyroid function and stable fluid and salt intake.

questions.rationale: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic range and requires systematic monitoring.

questions.sectionLabel: Psychopharmacology, Physical Health and Co-occurring Conditions
questions.stem: A patient taking an antipsychotic develops high fever, severe rigidity and altered consciousness. What should the nurse suspect?
questions.rationale: Fever, rigidity and altered consciousness are key warning signs of neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

questions.sectionLabel: Psychopharmacology, Physical Health and Co-occurring Conditions
questions.stem: Which adverse effect should be monitored with many antipsychotics?

options.text: Weight gain, glucose disturbance, lipid changes, movement disorders and cardiac risk.

questions.rationale: Antipsychotics may affect metabolic, neurological and cardiac health.

questions.sectionLabel: Psychopharmacology, Physical Health and Co-occurring Conditions
questions.stem: A patient becomes restless, sweaty, tremulous and hyperreflexic after an antidepressant dose increase. What should the nurse consider?
questions.rationale: The cluster is concerning for serotonin syndrome.

questions.sectionLabel: Psychopharmacology, Physical Health and Co-occurring Conditions
questions.stem: Why should physical-health screening be routine in severe mental illness?

options.text: People experience significant physical-health inequality and may have unrecognised cardiometabolic disease.
Physical health is managed only in primary care.
Screening is needed only before admission.

questions.rationale: Weight, blood pressure, glucose, lipids, smoking and preventive care should be addressed.

questions.sectionLabel: Psychopharmacology, Physical Health and Co-occurring Conditions
questions.stem: A patient taking an antipsychotic gains 12 kg and develops elevated glucose. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ignore the change because psychiatric stability is more important.
Escalate for metabolic review and support nutrition, activity and treatment discussion.

questions.rationale: Metabolic effects require active monitoring and multidisciplinary management.

questions.sectionLabel: Psychopharmacology, Physical Health and Co-occurring Conditions
questions.stem: A patient abruptly stops heavy alcohol use and develops agitation, sweating and tremor. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assess for severe withdrawal and arrange urgent medical management.

questions.rationale: Alcohol withdrawal can progress rapidly and may be life-threatening.

questions.sectionLabel: Psychopharmacology, Physical Health and Co-occurring Conditions
questions.stem: Which statement best reflects care for co-occurring substance use?

options.text: Both mental-health and substance-related needs should be assessed and managed together.
Substance use must be treated before mental illness.
The patient must stop all substances before receiving care.
Substance use is outside nursing scope.

questions.rationale: Integrated care avoids fragmented treatment.

questions.sectionLabel: Psychopharmacology, Physical Health and Co-occurring Conditions
questions.stem: A patient taking a sedating medicine is difficult to rouse. What should the nurse assess first?

options.text: Airway, breathing, oxygenation and level of consciousness.

questions.rationale: Excessive sedation may compromise breathing and requires urgent physiological assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Psychopharmacology, Physical Health and Co-occurring Conditions
questions.stem: A patient reports chest pain after stimulant use. What is the safest response?

options.text: Complete urgent physical assessment and escalate possible cardiovascular complications.
Focus on motivation to stop substances.

questions.rationale: Stimulant use can cause serious cardiovascular harm.

questions.sectionLabel: Psychopharmacology, Physical Health and Co-occurring Conditions
questions.stem: Which finding suggests movement-related antipsychotic adverse effects?

options.text: New tremor, rigidity or involuntary movements.

questions.rationale: Movement disorders require assessment and review.

questions.sectionLabel: Psychopharmacology, Physical Health and Co-occurring Conditions
questions.stem: A patient taking lithium begins a low-salt diet and intense exercise during hot weather. Why is this concerning?

options.text: Changes in salt and fluid balance may increase lithium levels and toxicity risk.
It has no relevance to lithium.

questions.rationale: Dehydration and altered sodium balance can increase lithium concentration.

questions.sectionLabel: Psychopharmacology, Physical Health and Co-occurring Conditions
questions.stem: Which nursing action supports cardiovascular health?

options.text: Regular blood pressure, weight, smoking and metabolic assessment with health-promotion support.
Leaving all physical care to medical staff.

questions.rationale: Whole-person care includes prevention and risk reduction.

questions.sectionLabel: Psychopharmacology, Physical Health and Co-occurring Conditions
questions.stem: A patient with depression reports new agitation and suicidal thoughts after starting an antidepressant. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Explain that this is always expected.
Assess risk urgently and communicate the possible activation effect.
Wait until the next routine appointment.

questions.rationale: Early activation or worsening suicidality requires prompt review.

questions.sectionLabel: Psychopharmacology, Physical Health and Co-occurring Conditions
questions.stem: A patient with opioid intoxication has slow breathing and reduced consciousness. What is the priority?

options.text: Emergency airway and breathing support and urgent medical response.

questions.rationale: Opioid overdose is a medical emergency.

questions.sectionLabel: Psychopharmacology, Physical Health and Co-occurring Conditions
questions.stem: Why should nurses avoid diagnostic overshadowing?

options.text: Physical symptoms may be wrongly attributed to mental illness, delaying treatment.
It applies only to older adults.

questions.rationale: Diagnostic overshadowing contributes to physical-health inequality.

questions.sectionLabel: Psychopharmacology, Physical Health and Co-occurring Conditions
questions.stem: A patient on antipsychotic treatment reports palpitations and fainting. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Assess urgently for possible cardiac adverse effects.
Wait for the next medication review.

questions.rationale: Palpitations and syncope may indicate significant cardiac risk.

questions.sectionLabel: Psychopharmacology, Physical Health and Co-occurring Conditions
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates integrated psychopharmacology care?

options.text: Benefits, adverse effects, blood tests, physical health and substance use are monitored together.

questions.rationale: Safe medication care is whole-person and ongoing.

questions.sectionLabel: Psychopharmacology, Physical Health and Co-occurring Conditions
questions.stem: A patient using several substances presents with confusion. What is the best approach?

options.text: Wait until the patient is sober.
Assess intoxication, withdrawal, physical illness, medicines and mental state together.

questions.rationale: Complex presentations require broad differential assessment.

questions.sectionLabel: Legal, Ethical and Culturally Safe International Practice
questions.stem: An international nurse is unsure whether a voluntary patient may leave the unit. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Check the patient’s legal status, local policy and senior advice before acting.
Use practice from the nurse’s home country.
Ask another patient what usually happens.

questions.rationale: Mental-health law differs across jurisdictions and must be confirmed locally.

questions.sectionLabel: Legal, Ethical and Culturally Safe International Practice
questions.stem: Which principle should guide involuntary care?

options.text: Lawful, proportionate and least restrictive care with review rights respected.

questions.rationale: Core principles include dignity, autonomy, proportionality and least restriction.

questions.sectionLabel: Legal, Ethical and Culturally Safe International Practice
questions.stem: A patient lacks decision-making capacity for one treatment. What should the nurse understand?

options.text: Capacity is permanently absent for all decisions.
The family automatically becomes the legal decision-maker.
Capacity is decision-specific and may change over time.

questions.rationale: Capacity should be assessed for the specific decision and context.

questions.sectionLabel: Legal, Ethical and Culturally Safe International Practice
questions.stem: A patient discloses a serious and immediate threat to another person. How should confidentiality be managed?

options.text: Keep the information secret in all circumstances.
Share information through lawful channels necessary to prevent serious harm and explain limits where possible.

questions.rationale: Confidentiality has lawful limits when serious harm is at stake.

questions.sectionLabel: Legal, Ethical and Culturally Safe International Practice
questions.stem: A family asks for information, but the patient has not consented. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Protect confidentiality, seek consent and share only what is lawfully permitted.
Share everything because family members provide support.
Refuse all communication with the family.
Ask the family to access the record.

questions.rationale: Family involvement must respect consent, confidentiality and safety.

questions.sectionLabel: Legal, Ethical and Culturally Safe International Practice
questions.stem: Which situation requires a professional interpreter?

options.text: A complex consent, risk or legal-status discussion when language barriers exist.
Any conversation regardless of language ability.

questions.rationale: Professional interpretation supports accuracy, consent and cultural safety.

questions.sectionLabel: Legal, Ethical and Culturally Safe International Practice
questions.stem: A patient’s family expects to make all treatment decisions, but the patient wishes to decide independently. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Follow the family’s cultural expectation automatically.
Explore the patient’s preferences and capacity, while respectfully discussing family roles.

questions.rationale: Cultural safety requires asking rather than assuming and prioritising the person’s rights.

questions.sectionLabel: Legal, Ethical and Culturally Safe International Practice
questions.stem: Which action is most trauma-informed?

options.text: Using surprise to avoid anticipatory anxiety.
Explaining what will happen, offering choices and avoiding unnecessary coercion.

questions.rationale: Trauma-informed care promotes safety, trust, choice and control.

questions.sectionLabel: Legal, Ethical and Culturally Safe International Practice
questions.stem: A patient under involuntary care requests information about review rights. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Provide accurate information according to local law and policy.
Refer the patient only after discharge.
Ask the family whether the review is appropriate.

questions.rationale: Patients retain legal rights and should receive clear information.

questions.sectionLabel: Legal, Ethical and Culturally Safe International Practice
questions.stem: Which documentation is most important when care is provided under mental-health legislation?

options.text: A general statement that the patient is detained.
Legal status, authority, assessments, decisions, restrictions, reviews and information provided.

questions.rationale: Legal care requires precise and contemporaneous documentation.

questions.sectionLabel: Legal, Ethical and Culturally Safe International Practice
questions.stem: A nurse assumes that a patient from a particular culture does not discuss suicide. What is the main problem?

options.text: Culture has no relevance to mental health.
It may prevent direct assessment and culturally safe care.

questions.rationale: Cultural safety requires respectful enquiry, not stereotypes.

questions.sectionLabel: Legal, Ethical and Culturally Safe International Practice
questions.stem: Which multidisciplinary practice best improves continuity?

options.text: Each discipline writes a separate plan.
The medical team makes all decisions.
Clear shared goals, named responsibilities and timely communication across settings.

questions.rationale: Defined roles and shared planning reduce fragmentation.

questions.sectionLabel: Legal, Ethical and Culturally Safe International Practice
questions.stem: A patient wants a spiritual leader involved. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Support involvement with consent and according to safety and service processes.
Decline because spirituality is outside healthcare.
Ask the spiritual leader to make decisions.

questions.rationale: Culturally responsive care may include spiritual support chosen by the person.

questions.sectionLabel: Legal, Ethical and Culturally Safe International Practice
questions.stem: An IQN is unfamiliar with local restraint law. What is the safest action?

options.text: Seek senior guidance and review policy before independent use except in immediate emergency actions within scope.

questions.rationale: Orientation to local law is essential before independent practice.

questions.sectionLabel: Legal, Ethical and Culturally Safe International Practice
questions.stem: Which statement best reflects autonomy?

options.text: Autonomy applies only to voluntary patients.
People should be involved in decisions as far as possible, with limits only when lawfully justified.

questions.rationale: Autonomy is fundamental but may be limited lawfully and proportionately.

questions.sectionLabel: Legal, Ethical and Culturally Safe International Practice
questions.stem: A family provides important relapse information, but the patient requests privacy. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ask the family to decide treatment.
Receive relevant information, protect confidentiality and discuss with the patient how support can be involved.

questions.rationale: Clinicians may receive information while still protecting what they disclose.

questions.sectionLabel: Legal, Ethical and Culturally Safe International Practice
questions.stem: Which question best supports cultural formulation?

options.text: “How do you understand what is happening, and who would you like involved?”
“Why do people from your culture believe this?”

questions.rationale: Open respectful questions explore meaning and preferences without stereotyping.

questions.sectionLabel: Legal, Ethical and Culturally Safe International Practice
questions.stem: A patient has hearing impairment and complex legal information must be discussed. What should the nurse arrange?

options.text: Appropriate accessible communication support and confirmation of understanding.

questions.rationale: Legal and consent discussions require accessible communication.

questions.sectionLabel: Legal, Ethical and Culturally Safe International Practice
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates safe family collaboration?

options.text: The family directs the care plan.
Family support is used appropriately while the patient’s consent, privacy and safety are respected.
The patient is excluded from discussion.

questions.rationale: Collaboration must balance support with rights and confidentiality.

questions.sectionLabel: Legal, Ethical and Culturally Safe International Practice
questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects safe international mental-health practice?

options.text: The nurse applies previous-country routines confidently.
The nurse uses local law, culturally safe communication, least restriction and clear multidisciplinary coordination.

questions.rationale: International practice requires local legal orientation, cultural responsiveness and coordinated care.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Recovery-Oriented and Rights-Based Services
questions.stem: A service audit shows that most care-plan goals are written by clinicians, while service users rarely contribute. Which leadership response best reflects recovery-oriented practice?

options.text: Co-design a revised planning process with people who use the service and measure participation at reviews.
Provide staff with a reminder to ask about goals.
Require service users to sign existing plans.
Ask families to write the goals instead.

questions.rationale: Recovery leadership requires systems that reflect personal goals, strengths and choice. Co-production and measurement are stronger than symbolic consultation.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Recovery-Oriented and Rights-Based Services
questions.stem: Which action is the clearest example of co-production?

options.text: Inviting one service user to endorse a completed policy.
Involving people with lived experience as equal partners in designing, delivering and evaluating a programme.
Asking staff to predict what service users would prefer.

questions.rationale: Co-production means meaningful partnership, not token representation or consultation after decisions are made.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Recovery-Oriented and Rights-Based Services
questions.stem: A nurse reports that staff avoid reflective supervision because they fear being judged. What should the leader do?

options.text: Create psychologically safe supervision with clear purpose, confidentiality boundaries and supportive facilitation.
Ask managers to record staff weaknesses.

questions.rationale: Reflective supervision should support learning and wellbeing rather than function as punishment.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Recovery-Oriented and Rights-Based Services
questions.stem: A person with psychosis is repeatedly denied routine physical-health review because staff attribute symptoms to mental illness. Which leadership issue is most relevant?
questions.rationale: Rights-based leadership challenges stigma and ensures equal access to physical healthcare.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Recovery-Oriented and Rights-Based Services
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates supported decision-making?

options.text: The person receives accessible information, support to express preferences and maximum participation in decisions.
The clinician chooses the safest option without discussion.
The person is asked to agree after the plan is finalised.

questions.rationale: Supported decision-making promotes autonomy while providing assistance needed for meaningful participation.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Recovery-Oriented and Rights-Based Services
questions.stem: A service advertises itself as recovery-oriented, but ward routines remain rigid and personal goals are rarely discussed. What should leaders conclude?

options.text: The service is recovery-oriented because the policy uses correct language.
Organisational routines are undermining stated recovery values.
The issue is limited to documentation.

questions.rationale: Recovery values must be visible in routines, communication, care planning and evaluation.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Recovery-Oriented and Rights-Based Services
questions.stem: Which measure would best evaluate whether a service is becoming more rights-based?

options.text: Service-user participation, complaints, supported decision-making, access to physical healthcare and restrictive-practice rates.

questions.rationale: A rights-based service should be evaluated through participation, equity, dignity and safety indicators.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Recovery-Oriented and Rights-Based Services
questions.stem: A team uses stigmatising shorthand during handover. What should the nurse leader do?

options.text: Ignore informal language if care remains safe.
Replace verbal handover with written notes.
Ask service users not to hear handover.
Challenge the language, model objective communication and include anti-stigma expectations in supervision and audit.

questions.rationale: Language shapes attitudes and care; leaders should address stigma in everyday systems.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Recovery-Oriented and Rights-Based Services
questions.stem: A family wants to participate in care, but the service user has not given consent. What is the best leadership standard?

options.text: Family involvement should respect consent, confidentiality and safety while still allowing general support and listening.
Ask the family to obtain legal authority.

questions.rationale: Partnership must be balanced with the person's rights and confidentiality.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Recovery-Oriented and Rights-Based Services
questions.stem: Which workforce strategy is most likely to preserve compassion in complex care?

options.text: Reflective supervision, debriefing, manageable workload and psychological safety.

questions.rationale: Compassion is supported by healthy systems, not by expecting individual resilience alone.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Recovery-Oriented and Rights-Based Services
questions.stem: A person with lived experience is invited to a committee but receives papers late and has no voting role. What is the main concern?

options.text: The person needs more clinical education.
Participation is tokenistic rather than meaningful.
Voting should remain restricted to professionals.

questions.rationale: Meaningful partnership requires access, influence and equitable participation.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Recovery-Oriented and Rights-Based Services
questions.stem: A leader wants to improve anti-stigma practice. Which intervention is strongest?

options.text: Removing diagnostic labels from all records.
Lived-experience education combined with policy review, language standards, outcome monitoring and accountability.

questions.rationale: Sustained anti-stigma action requires multiple system-level strategies.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Recovery-Oriented and Rights-Based Services
questions.stem: Which statement best reflects recovery leadership?

options.text: Leaders align language, routines, planning and evaluation with hope, identity, choice and strengths.
Leaders focus on symptom control above all else.
Leaders avoid risk discussion to preserve hope.
Leaders delegate recovery work to peer staff.

questions.rationale: Recovery leadership embeds recovery values throughout the service.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Recovery-Oriented and Rights-Based Services
questions.stem: A team member admits uncertainty after a difficult interaction. What should the leader do?

options.text: Record the concern for performance review.
Use reflective discussion to support learning while maintaining accountability.
Tell the nurse to be more confident.
Remove the nurse from direct care.

questions.rationale: Psychological safety allows uncertainty to be explored constructively.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Recovery-Oriented and Rights-Based Services
questions.stem: Which action best advances mental-health equity?

options.text: Focusing only on the majority population.
Examining access and outcomes across groups and adapting services where inequity is found.

questions.rationale: Equity requires identifying and addressing unequal access or outcomes.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Recovery-Oriented and Rights-Based Services
questions.stem: A service user says reviews feel rushed and decisions are made before the meeting. What should the leader do?

options.text: Ask the person to prepare more carefully.
Redesign reviews so information is shared beforehand and the person's goals guide discussion.

questions.rationale: Participation must be practical and timely, not symbolic.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Recovery-Oriented and Rights-Based Services
questions.stem: Which outcome best reflects psychologically safe leadership?

options.text: Staff speak up early, seek support and participate honestly in learning reviews.
Incidents are discussed privately by managers.

questions.rationale: Psychological safety is demonstrated through open reporting and learning.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Recovery-Oriented and Rights-Based Services
questions.stem: A service has strong clinical outcomes but repeated reports of coercive communication. What should leaders do?

options.text: Prioritise outcomes because communication is subjective.
Treat experience and dignity as quality indicators and redesign communication practice.
Refer all concerns to complaints staff.

questions.rationale: Rights-based quality includes how care is delivered, not only clinical outcomes.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Recovery-Oriented and Rights-Based Services
questions.stem: Which action best supports staff wellbeing after a serious event?

options.text: Timely debriefing, access to support and a fair learning process.
Requiring staff to return to normal duties immediately.

questions.rationale: Staff wellbeing and learning are supported through psychologically safe review.

questions.sectionLabel: Leading Recovery-Oriented and Rights-Based Services
questions.stem: Which outcome best demonstrates mature recovery-oriented leadership?

options.text: Clinicians retain final control over all plans.
People influence service design, staff feel safe to reflect and systems protect dignity, choice and equity.

questions.rationale: Mature leadership integrates partnership, workforce culture, rights and measurable system change.

questions.sectionLabel: Reducing Restrictive Practice and Strengthening Safety Systems
questions.stem: A unit has high restraint use during evening shifts. Data show crowding, limited activity, inconsistent staffing and delayed medication review. What should leaders do first?

options.text: Address the environmental and staffing contributors and evaluate trauma-informed alternatives.

questions.rationale: The pattern points to system conditions, not simply individual behaviour.

questions.sectionLabel: Reducing Restrictive Practice and Strengthening Safety Systems
questions.stem: Which data set is most useful when reviewing restrictive practice?

options.text: Frequency, duration, population, shift, trigger, intervention and outcome.

questions.rationale: Meaningful review requires context and disaggregation to identify patterns and inequity.

questions.sectionLabel: Reducing Restrictive Practice and Strengthening Safety Systems
questions.stem: A restraint event ends without physical injury. What should happen next?

options.text: Only the legal form should be completed.
The event should be reviewed for triggers, alternatives, experience and learning.
Staff should avoid discussing it with the person.

questions.rationale: Every restrictive event should prompt learning because psychological harm and system risk may remain.

questions.sectionLabel: Reducing Restrictive Practice and Strengthening Safety Systems
questions.stem: Which service feature is most consistent with trauma-informed care?

options.text: Strict uniform rules for all people.
Use of restriction to establish control.
Predictable routines, choice, collaboration and attention to sensory needs.

questions.rationale: Trauma-informed systems maximise safety, predictability, collaboration and choice.

questions.sectionLabel: Reducing Restrictive Practice and Strengthening Safety Systems
questions.stem: A suicide-prevention audit shows good inpatient assessment but poor follow-up after discharge. Which improvement should be prioritised?

options.text: Reliable transition communication, rapid follow-up and accessible crisis plans.

questions.rationale: Suicide prevention depends on continuity across transitions, not assessment alone.

questions.sectionLabel: Reducing Restrictive Practice and Strengthening Safety Systems
questions.stem: A service reports lower restraint use overall, but rates remain high among one ethnic group. What should leaders do?

options.text: Examine the inequity, involve the affected community and adapt practice.

questions.rationale: Disaggregated data may reveal inequity hidden by averages.

questions.sectionLabel: Reducing Restrictive Practice and Strengthening Safety Systems
questions.stem: Which intervention best reduces behavioural escalation?

options.text: Using medication as the first response.
Early engagement, meaningful activity, sensory support and clear communication.

questions.rationale: Prevention and early engagement are central to safer alternatives.

questions.sectionLabel: Reducing Restrictive Practice and Strengthening Safety Systems
questions.stem: A person in crisis says previous restraint was traumatic. What should the team do?

options.text: Explain that restraint may still be necessary.
Ask family to decide the plan.
Include triggers, preferences and alternatives in a collaboratively developed safety plan.
